newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian militants bomb bridge in fresh attack.
newsitem.headline: Indian militants bomb bridge in fresh attack.

text.p: Suspected tribal militants defied an army crackdown on Wednesday and blew up a railway bridge in the same region of northeastern India where two blasts tore through a passenger train this week.

Police said the explosion destroyed a small railway bridge about 160 km (100 miles) northeast of a spot where dozens of train passengers were killed on Monday in explosions that wrecked the Delhi-bound Brahmaputra Mail train.
No one was injured in Wednesday's explosion, which occurred in the early morning between Goreswar and Khoivabari towns, some 70 km (45 miles) west of Assam state's biggest city, Guwahati, they said.
A police spokesman in Kokrajhar, near the site of Monday's blasts, said Bodo tribal guerrillas were believed to have carried out both attacks.
The latest explosion severed a key railway link to northeastern tea- and oil-rich Assam and marked the third attack in four days by suspected Bodo guerrillas.

Monday's blasts cut the main rail line between northeastern India and the rest of the country, while an earlier attack on Sunday, also attributed to Bodo militants, had destroyed a bridge on a national highway, severing the main road link.
Railway officials said they expected the main rail line to be restored later on Wednesday.
Mainline Bodos want a separate province to be carved out of Assam, north of the Brahmaputra river. This week's attacks were blamed on a hardline fringe seeking a separate Bodo nation.
The latest attack came despite an army hunt for the Bodos.
"We are launching a major offensive against the separatist rebels," Brigadier K. Khare, in charge of regional army operations, told Reuters.
"We expect some encounters and explosions by separatists rebels. We are prepared to face this," he said. Khare did not disclose any details of the combing operation.
There was continuing confusion over how many people were killed in the attack on the train, which was packed with passengers heading off for New Year holidays.
Dilip Bora, railway spokesman in Guwahati, told Reuters that 33 bodies had been recovered.
But local officials said the official death toll did not take into account at least two dozen bodies that were pulled from the wreckage shortly after the blasts.
"It is possible that some persons took away bodies and those were not counted," Bora told Reuters. "We have counted only those taken away by railway authorities."
In the hours after the train attack, authorities said they believed at least 300 passengers had died.

"Since the area of the blast site is remote, it took time for the real figures to come out," Bora said. "The local journalists calculated figures based on the passenger capacity of the affected carriages."
Up to 300 passengers were in the three worst-hit carriages.
An army official who asked not to be named said the mutilated condition of many of the victims compounded confusion. "It's all flesh and one can't distinguish bodies," he said.
He said army officials suspected many more people had died, and the final toll might not be known until much later.
